title: Kunti repays the house
hook: in hiding at Ekachakra, Kunti hears her hosts weeping over whose turn it is to die, and offers her own son: a guest's debt, paid as dharma
carry: repaying kindness is dharma, not a favor

segments.voice: Yesterday, bhakti asks for God over comfort at the chariot, asking Krishna for troubles to come again, because in trouble she saw him.

Through a thin wall, in a borrowed room, a mother hears another family crying. Years before the war, after the house of lac burned, Kunti and her sons are hiding in a town called Ekachakra, dressed as poor brahmins, living with a brahmin family who took them in. One evening the house fills with weeping. Kunti goes to find out why. Tomorrow, the family tells her, it's their turn. A demon named Baka lives near the town, and each household in turn must send him a cart of food and a person to be eaten with it. Now they're arguing over who should go. Today: what Kunti says next.
screen: `A BORROWED ROOM IN EKACHAKRA.` → `THE HOST FAMILY WEEPS.` → `IT'S THEIR TURN TOMORROW.`

segments.voice: The scene is in the Mahabharata's first book, and it starts with the family. The father says he will go. The mother says no, she will; the children need their father more. The daughter says send me. And the small son picks up a blade of grass, waves it, and says he'll kill the demon with that. Then Kunti speaks, in paraphrase. You have sheltered us; let me repay you. I have five sons, and one of them will take the food to Baka. The brahmin refuses. He can't let a guest die for him. Kunti insists: the son she has in mind is strong. When the brothers come home, Yudhishthira is upset: you're risking our brother on a stranger's trouble? Kunti is calm. She has seen Bhima's strength since he was a baby. And repaying the people who sheltered them, she says, is dharma. So Bhima goes, eats the demon's food in front of him to make him angry, and kills him. Here's the teaching. Hinduism has a word for what Kunti is weighing: rina, debt. The Vedic texts say a person is born owing debts, to the gods, to the sages, to the ancestors; and the householder's daily duties include caring for people, the guest above all. Kunti is the guest here, and she owes. To her, paying it back isn't generosity she can skip. It's dharma. Her eldest questions her. The decision is hers.
screen: `EACH ONE OFFERS TO GO` · `LET ME REPAY YOU` · `RINA: THE DEBTS WE'RE BORN WITH` · `REPAYING THE HOUSE IS DHARMA`

segments.voice: Bring to mind a time someone took you in, a room, a meal, a ride, a hand when you needed it, and let their face come clearly. Hold them with each breath. Then let one small way to repay that kindness come to mind, a call, a meal, an hour of help, the way Hindu families have long answered kindness with food and time. If you pray, you can give thanks for them by name.
Kunti. In hiding at Ekachakra, she offered one of her own sons to repay the family who sheltered them, and called it dharma. Today's word.
Your line: repaying kindness is dharma, not a favor. Kunti owed the house. Go gently.

howItsDone: Hindus meet the Ekachakra story in retellings of the Mahabharata, in children's books and in storytelling, often told as Bhima's adventure, with Kunti's choice at its center.

chat.meaning: At Ekachakra Kunti weighs it calmly and calls repaying the family who sheltered them dharma. Hindu teaching speaks of rina, the debts every person carries, and kindness received is one to repay.

Ekachakra.meaning: the town where Kunti and her sons hid in disguise

Baka.meaning: the demon who demands food and a person from the town

Bhima.meaning: Kunti's strongest son, who goes to face Baka

Yudhishthira.meaning: Kunti's eldest son, who questions her choice

rina.meaning: debt; in Hindu teaching, what every person owes

sources.ref: Mahabharata, Adi Parva, the slaying of Baka (Bakavadha Parva; Critical Edition 1.145–152; Ganguli sections 157–166)
Mahabharata, Adi Parva (Pritha, given to King Kuntibhoja, called Kunti)
Taittiriya Samhita 6.3.10.5 (a person is born owing three debts: to the sages, the gods and the ancestors)
Shatapatha Brahmana 11.5.6.1 (the five great daily offerings, including to people: hospitality)

notes: Confirm the Ekachakra details: father, mother and daughter each offer to go; the small son brandishes a blade of grass; Kunti offers one of her five sons; the brahmin refuses to let a guest die; Yudhishthira objects and Kunti explains, citing Bhima's strength and the duty to repay the host; Bhima eats the food before Baka.
'She has seen Bhima's strength since he was a baby' alludes to the Adi Parva story of infant Bhima falling from Kunti's lap and shattering a rock; it is kept vague on purpose.
Mother's line 'he can find another wife' is a compressed paraphrase of her argument; check tone.
